stops.name: Saint-Denis, the armor laid before Our Lady
stops.campa: The king breaks the campaign; the bridge Alençon built over the Seine for a second assault is cut in the night by royal order. Before she is led away south, Jehanne hangs up her white harness and a sword won before Paris as an offering before the image of Our Lady at Saint-Denis, as wounded men-at-arms do: a soldier's ex-voto in the church whose name is the cry of France. It is the gesture of a vow suspended, not surrendered. The army that lifted Orléans and crowned the king is dissolved on the Loire within the fortnight; and the voices do not tell her why.
stops.quote: Out of devotion, as is the custom of men of war when they are wounded; and because I had been wounded before Paris; and because it was the cry of France.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, March 1431 (asked why she offered her arms at Saint-Denis)

stops.name: Gien, the army broken up
stops.campa: At Gien, where the coronation army was born in June, the king disbands it in September. Alençon goes home to Normandy's border; when he later asks for the Maid to campaign with him again, the council refuses. The chronicler of the house of Alençon writes the epitaph of the season: thus were broken the will of the Maid and the army of the king. She is kept henceforth near a court that fears her sword and cherishes her legend, given honors, a household, cloth-of-gold: everything but the war her voices commanded. Between her and Paris the ministers stretch their parchment truces.

stops.name: Bourges, three weeks in the house of Marguerite La Touroulde
stops.campa: In Bourges, capital of the once-mocked king, she lodges three weeks with Marguerite La Touroulde, wife of the receiver-general. Her hostess finds her simple as a child in everything but war and prayer: bathes with her at the steam-baths, sees her often in confession, watches her give alms with both hands; she was sent for the consolation of the poor, she says. Women crowd the house with rosaries for her to touch; she laughs at them: touch them yourselves. When Marguerite says she surely does not fear battle, knowing she will not be killed, she answers that she is no surer of that than any soldier.
stops.quote: Touch them yourselves — your touch will do them as much good as mine.
stops.quote_source: Testimony of Marguerite La Touroulde, rehabilitation trial (1456)

stops.name: Saint-Pierre-le-Moûtier, the fifty thousand
stops.campa: Sent at last against the freebooter Perrinet Gressart's towns, she assaults Saint-Pierre-le-Moûtier. The storm is thrown back; the retreat sounds; her squire d'Aulon, himself wounded, sees her left almost alone by the moat and rides to drag her away. Why does she stay? She lifts her visor and speaks the sentence of the hidden army: she is not alone; fifty thousand of her own are in her company, and she will not leave until the town is taken. Then: to the fagots and hurdles, all of you, and bridge the moat! It is bridged, the town is stormed, and no one understands it except that it happened.
stops.quote: I am not alone: I have still in my company fifty thousand of my men; and I shall not leave this spot until I have taken the town.
stops.quote_source: Testimony of Jean d'Aulon, rehabilitation trial (1456)

stops.name: La Charité-sur-Loire, the siege that fails
stops.campa: Before the strong town of La Charité, Gressart's own den on the Loire, the royal siege sits down in the cold with too little powder, money, or will from the court. She writes to the good towns begging powder, saltpetre and sulphur; Riom promises and does not send. After a month of frost the siege is raised and the guns are left in the mud: the first enterprise of the Maid to fail outright, and the counselors mark it. In December the king ennobles her and all her blood with the lily and the name du Lys; the honor gilds the bridle as the reins are drawn in.
stops.quote: Who told you that I had a command from God to enter La Charité?
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 3 March 1431

stops.name: Sully-sur-Loire, the gilded cage and the letters of spring
stops.campa: The winter closes over her in La Trémoille's own castle of Sully, where the court keeps her like a relic while Burgundy gathers to take Compiègne. From Sully her letters go out in March like birds ahead of a thaw: to the Hussites of Bohemia, threatening a crusade of her own if they do not return to the faith; twice to the anxious citizens of Reims, promising she will never abandon them while she lives. Before April she is gone: riding out without leave, without farewell to the king, with her brother and a free company, north toward the war that never signed the truces.
stops.quote: My dear and good friends... I promise and certify to you that I will not abandon you as long as I live.
stops.quote_source: Letter to the citizens of Reims, 16 March 1430

stops.name: Lagny-sur-Marne, Franquet d'Arras and the child restored
stops.campa: At Lagny on the Marne, among men who fight well for the kingdom of France, she takes the field again and breaks the Burgundian routier Franquet d'Arras, who is tried and beheaded for his murders. And at Lagny the canon records a miracle in her own voice: a child three days dead, black as her coat, is carried before the image of Our Lady where the maidens of the town are praying. Jehanne kneels and prays with them; colour returns, the infant yawns three times, is baptized, dies truly, and is buried in consecrated ground: a soul caught back from limbo for the length of a sacrament.
stops.quote: The child was three days dead... I was praying with the other maidens before the image of Our Lady, and at last life appeared in him; he yawned three times, and was then baptized; and soon he died, and was buried in consecrated ground.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 3 March 1431

stops.name: Melun, the voices foretell the capture
stops.campa: Melun casts out its Burgundian garrison at her coming, in Easter week. Walking on the town ditches, she receives from Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret the hardest of all their messages: she will be taken prisoner before Saint John's Day; it must be so; she must not be astonished, but accept it with a good heart, and God will help her. She begs that she may die quickly when taken, without the long travail of prison; the voices answer only: take everything with a good grace, it must be thus. From this day she stands under a sentence she alone can read, and she rides north anyway.
stops.quote: In Easter week last, when I was on the ditches of Melun, I was told by my voices — that is, by Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret — that I should be taken prisoner before Saint John's Day; and that so it must be; and that I should not be dismayed, but take all in good part, and God would help me.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 10 March 1431

stops.name: Compiègne, entry into the besieged city
stops.campa: Burgundy has come down on Compiègne, the loyal city that refused to be handed over by treaty. Jehanne swears the good sentence the chronicles keep, that she will see her good friends of Compiègne, and rides into the town at dawn with her free lances, welcomed with wine and processions by the townsmen who know what her presence is worth. She spends the fortnight striking at the besiegers' web: Pont-l'Évêque, Soissons, where a traitor captain shuts the bridge against her, and sells the town within days. Thinned to a few hundred, her company turns back for Compiègne. Saint John's Day is five weeks away.

stops.name: Margny, before Compiègne: the capture
stops.campa: At dawn she hears mass at Saint-Jacques and, the town's memory keeps, tells the children round the pillar that she is sold and betrayed and will soon be given to death. At five in the evening she leads a sortie over the bridge against Margny, in a huque of crimson and gold. Twice she drives the Burgundians; then Luxembourg's main force closes. She holds the rearguard on the causeway, last of all, crying to the retreating men to strike. The town's drawbridge rises behind her. An archer of the Bastard of Wandomme drags her from her horse by the golden coat. The prophecy of Melun is accomplished.
stops.quote: Think only of striking at them!... It shall rest with you alone that they are discomfited.
stops.quote_source: Perceval de Cagny, Chroniques (her words in the sortie)

stops.name: Beaulieu-lès-Fontaines, first prison, first escape
stops.campa: Jean de Luxembourg lodges his prize in his castle of Beaulieu-lès-Fontaines, in Vermandois. Her squire d'Aulon, captive with her and serving her still, mourns that Compiègne will fall; she answers that it will not: no place the King of Heaven has put in the hands of King Charles by her means will be lost. She squeezes between two planks of her prison toward the door of the yard, and would have locked her guards in the tower, had not the porter crossed her path. It is lawful, she will maintain to her judges' faces, for any prisoner to escape. They move her deeper into Burgundian land.
stops.quote: It is true that I wished to escape, and so I would from any prison; for I have never been a prisoner anywhere but that I would gladly escape. It is lawful for any prisoner to escape.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 15 March 1431

stops.name: Beaurevoir, the three ladies and the leap from the tower
stops.campa: Four months in Luxembourg's tower at Beaurevoir, where three ladies of the house, aunt, wife, stepdaughter, all named Jeanne, grow to love her and offer cloth for a woman's dress; she would have yielded to them sooner than to any lady of France save her queen. Then word comes that Compiègne is to be put to fire and sword, and that she is sold to the English. Against Saint Catherine's daily counsel she commends herself to God and leaps from the tower, sixty feet, and is found by the wall unbroken, senseless, unbleeding. Saint Catherine bids her be comforted: Compiègne shall have succour. She eats again.
stops.quote: I did it not out of despair, but in the hope of saving my body and of going to succour the good people in need... And after I had fallen, the voice of Saint Catherine told me to be of good cheer, for they of Compiègne would have succour.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 14 March 1431
